To reconvene means to come together as a group again after a break or pause — or to cause a group to come together again after that break.

Think of it in two parts:

  • "Re-" = again
  • "Convene" = to assemble or gather, especially for a formal purpose

So reconvene simply means: to assemble again.
What Makes Reconvene the Right Word

Not every re-gathering of people is a "reconvening." Three things must be true:

  1. A group had already met before — there was a prior session or meeting.
  2. That meeting was interrupted or paused — by a break, a recess, a suspension, or an adjournment.
  3. The group now comes back together — to continue what was started.

If any of these is missing, "reconvene" isn't the right fit. You can't reconvene something that never met in the first place. The word carries the idea of resumption — picking up where things were left off.
Two Ways to Use It

Reconvene works in two ways in a sentence:

1. The group reconvenes on its own (no one "causes" it — it just happens):

  • "The committee will reconvene at 3 PM."
  • "Parliament reconvened after the winter recess."

Here, the subject (the committee, Parliament) is doing the reconvening itself — coming back together.

2. Someone reconvenes the group (a person calls the group back):

  • "The judge reconvened the court after the lunch break."
  • "The chairperson reconvened the session the following morning."

Here, a person in authority is causing the group to come back together. They are making it happen.

Both uses are equally correct and common.
The Break Can Be Short or Long

One important thing to understand: the pause or break between the two sessions can be any length of time.

  • Minutes: "After a short recess, the jury reconvened."
  • Hours: "The negotiators reconvened after dinner."
  • Days: "The summit reconvened on Thursday."
  • Weeks or months: "Congress reconvened in January after its summer recess."

The word works across all these timeframes. What matters is that there was a gap — not how long it was.
Where You'll Commonly See It

"Reconvene" belongs to slightly formal settings — places where gatherings are taken seriously and organized. You'll encounter it most often in:

  • Courts of law — judges reconvene proceedings after breaks or adjournments
  • Parliaments and legislatures — after recesses or holidays
  • Business meetings and board sessions — especially longer ones with scheduled breaks
  • International negotiations and peace talks — when talks are suspended and then resumed
  • Academic conferences — sessions that continue after a break
  • Committees and task forces — groups that meet repeatedly over time

You could technically use it informally ("our book club reconvened at Sarah's house"), but in practice, the word carries a slightly formal, official tone.
A Crucial Distinction: It's Always About a Group

Reconvene always refers to multiple people coming together. One person cannot reconvene. You reconvene with others, or a group reconvenes as a whole.

Also, reconvene is specifically about people gathering — not about resuming a task by yourself. You might resume writing an essay after a break, but you reconvene with your co-authors.
How It Differs from Similar Words

WordWhat it implies
MeetA fresh gathering — no prior session assumed
ReconveneA return to a gathering — always implies a previous session and a break
ResumeTo continue something (a task, a journey, a conversation) — not specifically about a group assembling
RegroupTo come together again, but more informal and often after difficulty or disorder — doesn't necessarily imply a scheduled or formal session
A Range of Example Sentences

• "The meeting adjourned at noon and reconvened at 1:30 PM."
  • "After months of failed negotiations, the two sides finally agreed to reconvene."
  • "The judge told the jury to reconvene the next morning to continue deliberations."
  • "Parliament will reconvene next week to debate the new bill."
  • "The conference broke for lunch and reconvened at 2 o'clock for the afternoon panel."
  • "Both teams asked to reconvene after reviewing the data separately."
The Tone It Carries

When you use "reconvene," it signals:

  • The gathering is purposeful — people aren't just hanging out again, they're returning to business
  • There is unfinished work — something was left incomplete that the group is returning to address
  • The reassembly is expected or planned — it's not a surprise reunion, it's a continuation

This is why it feels slightly formal. It implies organization, process, and continuity.
In a Nutshell

Reconvene = a group that was meeting, paused, and has now come back together to continue.

It's the word for every courtroom after a recess, every parliament after a holiday, every boardroom after a lunch break — when the people walk back in, take their seats, and get back to it. That moment of reassembly, that return to the table? That's reconvening.
